n: Perhaps spoken at a harvest festival: don’t celebrate like the pagan nations. Israel has been unfaithful, treating harvest as a reward from Baal on every threshing floor.

f.w: thou hast loved a reward upon every cornfloor
f.g: Prized grain at harvest as a harlot’s fee from Baal.
Threshing floor, where grain was separated at harvest.

n: The threshing floor and winepress will not sustain them; the new wine will fail.
They won’t remain in the Lord’s land. Ephraim will go back to “Egypt”—bondage—and eat ritually unclean food in Assyria. Exile meant losing the ability to live by the Law.

f.w: they shall eat unclean things in Assyria

n: In exile they can’t offer proper sacrifices. Their food will be like mourners’ bread—unclean because it was in a house of death. It will feed only themselves and never reach God’s house.

f.g: Food in a house where someone died was ritually unclean.

n: What will they do on the festival days, far from the land and temple, unable to celebrate?
Fleeing destruction, they will die in Egypt and be buried at Memphis—famous for its huge cemeteries. Weeds and thorns will overgrow their treasured homes.

f.g: An ancient Egyptian capital known for its necropolis (city of tombs).

n: The days of punishment have come. The people mock the prophet as a fool and the inspired man as a madman—because their sin and hostility run so deep.

f.w: the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad

f.g: A time when God comes to judge.

n: The prophet is meant to be Ephraim’s watchman with God, but people set traps for him everywhere, even in God’s house. Hostility to the prophet is hostility to God.
Their corruption is as deep as at Gibeah, where a horrifying crime once led to civil war. God will remember and punish.

f.w: as in the days of Gibeah

n: God fondly remembers finding Israel long ago—like grapes found in the desert or the first ripe figs, a delightful surprise. But at Baal-peor they devoted themselves to shameful idolatry and became as vile as what they loved.

f.g: They became like the thing they loved.

n: Ephraim’s glory—its children and future—will fly away like a bird. No births, no pregnancies, no conceptions. Ephraim’s name relates to fruitfulness, making this especially pointed.

f.w: their glory shall fly away like a bird
f.g: Ephraim means “doubly fruitful”—now that fruitfulness will vanish.

n: Even if they raise children, they will lose them. Worst of all: woe to them when God departs!

f.w: woe also to them when I depart from them

n: Ephraim was planted in a pleasant place like Tyre, but will bring out its children to be slaughtered.

f.g: Tyre, a wealthy, beautifully situated Phoenician city.

n: Hosea, agonized, prays: what should You give them? Better barren wombs than children born only to die in war. This is a cry of grief, not cruelty.

f.w: a miscarrying womb and dry breasts

n: Their wickedness centers at Gilgal, a place of corrupt worship. There God came to “hate” them—reject them—and will drive them from His house. Their leaders are rebels.
Ephraim is struck like a plant whose root is dried up—no more fruit. Even their beloved children will perish.

“My God” will reject them because they did not listen; they will become wanderers among the nations. This describes the scattering of the northern ten tribes after 722 BC—whom Latter-day Saints believe God will gather again.

f.w: they shall be wanderers among the nations

f.g: Hosea speaks personally: Israel has rejected Him, but He is still Hosea’s God.
